name: e01 starter model and constant-share reference
expectation:
Starter: top choice matched about 29% (build) and 28% (check), as run_baseline.py prints.
I expect its log loss to be WORSE than the constant-share reference, because its weights are
hand-set and it underpredicts the entrant (15.9% vs 21.1%). Constant reference log loss should
be near the entropy of the shares, about 1.59 on build.

outputs.note: The starter is not trained on any data, so scoring it on check uses up nothing.

verdict: WRONG expectation: starter log loss 1.579 beats the constant reference 1.594 on build (and 1.563 vs 1.591 on check). But only by about 1%, so the hand-set weights carry very little signal. Bar for any new model: clearly below 1.58.

name: e02 household bootstrap of lever gaps
expectation:
Price: $3.49 minus $5.49 entrant share interval excludes zero, roughly +10 to +22 points.
Message: environment minus low_odor is borderline; I expect the lower end of the interval near 0.
Cleaning vs the others: interval includes zero.
Channel: online minus retail is borderline, lower end near or below 0.
Household resampling gives wider intervals than visit resampling, by 10-30%.
verdict: MIXED. Price confirmed: 3.49 vs 5.49 = +16.1 pts [11.2, 21.1]. Clustering concern WRONG for gaps: household and visit intervals are the same width (ratio 0.91-1.03), because each household saw several levels, so its own taste cancels in a gap. Households do differ (entrant-count variance 1.58 vs 1.00 binomial), so clustering still matters for levels. By my FIRST.md rule, environment vs low_odor [1.8, 13.4] and online vs retail [0.8, 9.5] pass. But I picked environment vs low_odor because it was the largest raw gap, and 7 gaps were tested; both lower ends are close to 0. I do NOT yet treat message or channel as settled. Next: a stricter test declared in advance.

name: e03 grow the learned model one idea at a time
expectation:
(I already fit model A once while testing the code: train log loss 1.58, price weight -0.46.)
A: cross-validated log loss about 1.585, no better than the starter (1.579).
B: usual brand helps clearly, CV log loss about 1.55, usual-brand weight about +0.5.
B+msg and B+chan: each improves CV log loss by less than 0.003, maybe none.

RULE, decided now: I call message or channel "real" only if BOTH
  (1) its Wald test inside model C has p < 0.01 (strict, because I test several things), and
  (2) adding it to B lowers cross-validated log loss.
My guess: message p between 0.01 and 0.1 and channel p about 0.03, so both FAIL the rule.
verdict: MOSTLY CONFIRMED, one surprise. A = 1.587 as guessed. Usual brand weight +0.49 as guessed, but B only reaches 1.575, not the 1.55 I expected: knowing the household helps much less than I thought. Message p=0.057 and channel p=0.026, both fail the pre-declared rule (p<0.01 AND lower CV loss); CV gains are tiny (0.0009 and 0.0004). Big lesson: every model sits near 1.575-1.59, so most of each choice is not predictable from these fields. Tight budget makes price matter a bit more (-0.083 +/- 0.043), not clear.

name: e04 does history help
expectation:
Stage 1 showed households repeat their last choice only 23.1% vs 20.6% by chance, so:
same_as_last_visit small and positive (about +0.15), not clear (p > 0.05).
none_after_buying_last_visit near zero (the starter assumes it is positive; I doubt it).
entrant_bought_before positive; entrant_bad_note_before negative.
Overall D improves CV log loss over C (1.5741) by less than 0.005.
RULE: history is worth carrying between visits only if D beats C in CV log loss.
verdict: PARTLY WRONG. History helps a little: CV 1.5741 -> 1.5701, rule passes. But the gain comes from ONE thing: entrant_bought_before +0.56 (z=3.4). same_as_last_visit is 0.00, not +0.15 as I guessed. none_after_buying is ~0 (z=0.5), so the starter's built-in idea is not supported. Bad entrant note -0.82 (z=-1.9) on only 51 visits: a hint, not proof. CAVEAT: 'bought before' may just mean some households liked the entrant from the start; this data cannot tell taste from 'trying it made them like it'. What the model carries between visits: did they buy the entrant before, and what note they gave it.

name: e05 options table with uncertainty
expectation:
$3.49 gives the highest entrant share in over 99% of resamples.
environment is the best message in about 70% of resamples; low_odor best in under 5%.
online beats retail in about 98% of resamples.
Best option (3.49, environment, online) has entrant share about 30-35%.
Revenue per shopper is also highest at $3.49.
Break-even cost per bottle for $4.49 over $3.49 is about $1.50, with a wide interval.
So the best PRICE for profit depends on a cost we do not know.

inputs.model: D = brand, price, household, levers, history

verdict: MOSTLY CONFIRMED. 3.49 has the most entrant share in 100% of resamples; online beats retail in 98.5%; environment is the best message in 81.5% (cleaning 17.5%, low_odor 1%). Best option 3.49/environment/online = 32.1% share [25%, 38%]. Revenue per shopper is highest at 3.49 (1.12 vs 1.04 at 4.49). SURPRISE: break-even cost per bottle for 4.49 over 3.49 is only 1.16 [0.11, 1.79], not ~1.50. If a bottle costs the brand more than ~1.16, 4.49 makes more profit; above ~2.36, 5.49 does. We do not know the cost, so the PROFIT-best price is unknown. CONFLICT to explain: run 3 says messages are not proven different (p=0.057), here environment wins 81.5% of resamples. Both are true: environment is the most likely winner, but a 1-in-5 chance it is not is too high to call it settled. These are first-visit shares only; no repeat or after-use effects.

name: e06 can we trust said_why
expectation:
"I bought the cleaner I often buy" matches the survey usual brand in at least 70% of cases.
"I know this brand/cleaner" shows up on some first-ever entrant purchases (over 5%): a clear contradiction.
"none" reasons said alongside a purchase: under 5%.
"less waste"/"refillable" come from entrant buyers over 90% of the time, and entrant buyers give
them about twice as often when the shelf said "environment".
People who bought nothing answer less often than buyers.
Overall: most answers fit the facts, but 10-25% of checkable answers contradict them.
So said_why is a weak hint, not the truth, and I will not use it as a model input.
verdict: PARTLY WRONG, and more useful than expected. Only 7.8% of checkable answers contradict facts (I guessed 10-25%). But the bigger finding: 15 of 16 reasons always come with ONE product (e.g. 'I know this brand' = always standard, 'I wanted less smell' = always entrant). Knowing the reason gives the choice 94.1% of the time (build), 95.7% (check: I looked at the check set's said_why mapping only for this count, no model decision used it). So said_why mostly repeats each product's own claims; it is not an independent 'why'. Contradictions sit in 2 reasons: 'I bought the cleaner I often buy' disagrees with the survey usual brand 9 of 31 times; 'I still had cleaner at home' after buying nothing last visit 7 of 18. Message priming guess WRONG: entrant buyers give waste/refill reasons LESS under environment (36%) than cleaning (46%) or low_odor (50%), small n. Entrant buyers answer more often (28.9% vs 20.8% budget). Decision: do not use said_why as a model input or as the household-level reason.

name: e07 one-time check set test of locked model D
expectation:
PASS RULES, decided now:
 (1) D log loss on check is lower than the starter (1.5626) AND the constant model (1.5905).
 (2) D's predicted entrant share is within 3 points of the real check share (18.3%).
 (3) Raw check data: entrant share at $3.49 is above $5.49.
Message and channel directions on check are reported but cannot pass or fail anything:
with about 100 visits per message, they are too noisy to settle it.
My guesses: D about 1.555, beating the starter by less than 0.01, and the household
interval for "D minus starter" probably includes zero. Entrant share predicted about 20%.
Price direction holds. environment > low_odor and online > retail: I think they hold, but weakly.

inputs.model: D = brand, price, household, levers, history

verdict: CONFIRMED VIEW (all 3 pre-declared rules pass). D log loss 1.552 vs starter 1.563 vs constant 1.591. Gain of 0.011 is small and the household interval [-0.038, +0.015] includes zero, as guessed: D is better on average but not proven better on 50 households. Entrant share predicted 21.0% vs actual 18.3% (2.6 pts, inside the 3-pt rule): D slightly OVERSELLS the entrant; the 15-25% bin predicts 19.7% but only 13.4% buy. Price direction strong on new households: 25.5% at 3.49 vs 7.7% at 5.49. Message and channel point the same way as in build (environment 21.9% vs 17.9%; online 22.2% vs 14.3%), which supports them but cannot settle them at ~100 visits each. The check set is now USED; any later result on it is not a fresh test.
